title: You Still Can't Fix Culture. Change What Keeps Producing It.
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Ten years after writing a widely-read piece arguing that organizational culture 'emerges' rather than being directly fixable, Claydon revisits and extends the argument, contending that culture is better understood as 'the patterned residue of people acting through roles within an organisational system' -- the accumulated result of structures, incentives, histories, and power relationships repeating themselves daily. He traces how the 1980s 'strong culture' movement, which promised alignment through shared values and inspirational leadership, gradually became an all-purpose explanation for every organizational problem until it lost its explanatory value, softening from mythic language into aesthetic branding while the underlying machinery of decision rights and incentives kept operating unchanged underneath. Central to the piece is a framework called 'Self-in-Role-in-System,' where roles act as a hinge translating systemic contradictions into lived tension for individuals, producing recognizable character-responses -- the zealot, the old guard, the bewildered, the strained, and the buffoon -- that Claydon argues are diagnostic signals rather than mere negativity. The essay's final extension addresses AI directly: as algorithms and generative models join the organisation as participants that observe, recommend, and act, Claydon argues they inherit and accelerate the same contradictions embedded in existing systems, meaning culture-change work must now focus on interpreting, mobilizing around, and experimenting with the underlying conditions that generate behavior.
points: Reframes the decade-old 'you can't fix culture' argument by adding a mechanism: culture is 'the patterned residue of people acting through roles within an organisational system,' produced daily through structures, incentives, and repeated decisions.

Traces how the 1980s 'strong culture' movement went from powerful diagnostic tool to explaining everything until the term lost explanatory value and softened into aesthetic branding like open offices and foosball tables.

Introduces 'Self-in-Role-in-System' as a framework where organizational roles act as a hinge that translates systemic contradictions into lived tension, producing recognizable character-responses like the zealot, the bewildered, and the buffoon.

Argues that as AI systems join organizations as active participants, they inherit and accelerate existing contradictions at machine speed, meaning culture work must shift toward interpreting and experimenting with underlying conditions rather than issuing new values statements.
quotes: Its argument was simple. Culture emerged from how the organisation actually worked. Values workshops, leadership speeches and change programmes played supporting roles. Daily organisational life did the real work.
Culture is the patterned residue of people acting through roles within an organisational system. That gives culture its diagnostic value.
Successful organisation? Study the culture. Failing organisation? Change the culture. Merger struggling? Integrate the cultures. Strategy stalled? Build a performance culture.
When everything became cultural, culture lost its explanatory value. It became an organisational Rorschach test.
An executive may be asked to act for the enterprise while being rewarded for protecting a function. A manager may carry accountability for an outcome while authority remains several levels above.

A fragmented organisation can produce faster fragmentation. A confused organisation can automate confusion. A political organisation can encode yesterday's distribution of power into tomorrow's intelligent workflow.
Culture becomes useful when we treat it as evidence. A pattern has appeared. People are behaving in recognisable ways.
